cases.why:
THE case #180 is written about. Two modules each declaring a PRIVATE Type of the same name, with different members. The issue asserts VB6 treats them as two unrelated types; if that is right then detecting the clash WITHOUT honouring visibility would refuse a legal program, which is the damaging direction and means #180 cannot be fixed without visibility. If instead VB6 refuses this, the fix is far simpler. Nothing in the corpus establishes it, and one module cannot ask.

NOTE ON THE HARNESS: Module1 declares Option Explicit deliberately. Without it an unresolvable name is simply an implicitly-declared Variant and the module compiles, so 'not found' and 'found unambiguously' are indistinguishable - which silently turned the first run of this case into a confident wrong fact. Option Explicit is what makes the probe able to fail.

The same collision with both PUBLIC. If two Publics clash and two Privates do not, visibility is exactly the discriminator and the procedure algorithm transfers unchanged. Measured separately because the two need not behave alike.

The mixed case, and the one that decides precedence: a module declaring its own Private Type while another exports a Public one of the same name. The procedure rule is 'own module first at any visibility, then other modules' Public only'. If Types follow it, the local Private wins and this compiles.

The Enum twin of the first case. Enums and Types are aggregated by the same code here, so if they diverge in VB6 the single program-wide table is wrong for a second reason.

A member name declared by enums in DIFFERENT modules, used bare. Within one module this is measured 'Ambiguous name detected' at the use. Across modules it may be the same, or the local one may win. Decides whether the ambiguity set is per-module or program-wide.

A bare member of a PRIVATE enum in another module. Predicting illegal - that is what Private means - and it is the control that shows visibility is actually enforced on members rather than only on the enum name.

The case the first round could not reach: the using module declares NO Point of its own, so there is nothing local to win and the name must come from elsewhere. With one exporter this should simply resolve. Its value is as the control for the next case, which adds a second exporter.

A first version used TypeName(p) and failed on an unrelated rule - a UDT cannot be passed to a late-bound function - which is a probe measuring its own mistake. Reading a field instead keeps the case about scoping.

THE case that decides whether an ambiguity rule applies to Types at all. Two OTHER modules each export a Public Type of the same name and the using module declares none, so nothing local can disambiguate. If VB6 refuses this, Types follow the procedure rule ('own module first, then other modules Public only, 2+ is ambiguous') and HexIDE can reuse that algorithm outright. If VB6 accepts it, Types are resolved by some other rule and the procedure algorithm does NOT transfer.

Two modules export the same Public Type, which is measured 'Ambiguous name detected' for the BARE name - so is the module-qualified form the escape hatch? If it is, the ambiguity is a property of the reference rather than of the declarations, and a resolver must accept a dotted type name in a Dim ... As position (the grammar's complexType already allows one). If it is not, then two exporters make the name unusable from that module at all, which is a much stronger statement.

The control: only ONE module exports Point, so nothing needs disambiguating. This separates 'the qualified form resolves an ambiguity' from 'the qualified form is accepted at all' - if this one fails too, the previous case says nothing about ambiguity.

The enum twin. Two modules export the same Public Enum and the reference names the module. The three-part form is already measured legal for a single declaring module; this asks whether it also RESOLVES an ambiguity, which is the property that matters for a design that has to decide when to raise.

A bare MEMBER name declared by enums in two different modules, qualified with one of those modules. Distinct from the previous case because here the enums have different names and only the member collides - so the module prefix is the only thing that can disambiguate, and there is no enum name to fall back on.
